category: Agent, instrument, means, manner, and measure

entries.ipa: /æt ðə bɪˈhɛst ʌv/ · weak /ət ðə bəˈhɛst əv/ · casually /ət ðə bəˈhɛst ə/, with the of down to a bare schwa
entries.register: formal to neutral; standard in journalism, history, and legal writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, and like the other agent phrases the complement must be animate or institutional — a person, an office, an agency. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand. With a pronoun the possessive construction is commoner: at his behest rather than at the behest of him.
entries.pattern: [passive clause] at the behest of [instigator] / At the behest of [instigator], [clause] / [clause] at [possessive] behest
entries.contrast: The one phrase in this section that names who ordered it rather than who did it. Plain by marks the hand; at the behest of marks the voice behind the hand, which is why the memo was written by a staffer at the behest of the governor can put two different agents in one sentence and no other construction can. Against on the part of: that phrase hangs an abstract noun on its doer, this one hangs a completed act on its instigator. Behest is a fossil noun exactly like dint in by dint of — it survives only inside this phrase, so it takes no plural and no modifier: not a strong behest, not at several behests.
variants: at the request of (the neutral everyday form)
at the urging of / at the insistence of (grading the pressure upward)
at the instigation of (the most accusatory and the rarest)
at the direction of (the civilian softening of military by direction of)
entries.meaning: Names the party whose request or order set the action going. It leaves the doer in place and adds a second, superior agent above them, which is why it is the standard phrase for reporting influence, pressure, and chains of command.
examples: The investigation was reopened at the behest of two members of the committee.
At the behest of the state, the district rewrote its attendance policy over the summer.
The clause was inserted at the behest of a single lender and nobody else read it closely.
She took the job at the behest of a mentor she could not say no to.
The audit was commissioned at his behest and delivered to him alone.
The park was renamed at the urging of a neighborhood association that had been asking for nine years.

entries.ipa: /æt ðə ˈhændz ʌv/ · weak /ət ðə ˈhændz əv/ · casually /ət ðə ˈhændz ə/, with the of down to a bare schwa
entries.register: neutral to formal; heavy in journalism and history writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, and the complement must be animate or institutional — a person, a group, a government, a team. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [noun of suffering] at the hands of [agent] / [passive verb of suffering] at the hands of [agent]
entries.contrast: A specialized by. It marks the agent only of something bad — defeat, injury, humiliation, death — and casts that agent as a perpetrator. He was killed by his brother is neutral reporting; He died at the hands of his brother is an accusation. The complement must be animate, so it cannot cover instruments or natural forces: not killed at the hands of a falling tree.
entries.meaning: Attributes harm to a responsible party. The phrase does rhetorical work that plain by does not: it foregrounds the agent, implies the suffering was inflicted rather than merely caused, and invites the reader to assign blame. Sportswriting borrowed it for defeats. 1. Suffering, injury, or death inflicted by someone. 2. Defeat in a contest.
examples: Thousands died at the hands of the regime in the first eighteen months alone.
She described years of mistreatment at the hands of a supervisor everyone had complained about.
He lost the house at the hands of a servicer that had misplaced two years of payments.
The team suffered its worst loss in a decade at the hands of a program it had beaten nine straight times.
The bill died at the hands of a committee that never scheduled a hearing on it.
Her first campaign ended at the hands of an incumbent nobody thought was vulnerable.

entries.ipa: /ˈkɚtəsi ʌv/ · weak /ˈkɚtəsi əv/ · casually /ˈkɚtəsi ə/, which is one reason the bare credit-line form courtesy the Newberry Library got written down
entries.register: neutral; standard in captions, credits, and journalism
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun naming a person, institution, or source. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It frequently appears with no verb at all, as a freestanding credit line.
entries.pattern: [clause] courtesy of [source] / [noun phrase], courtesy of [source] / Courtesy of [source] (caption)
entries.contrast: Against by: by credits authorship, courtesy of credits permission or supply — a photograph by Ansel Adams versus a photograph courtesy of the Adams estate. Against thanks to: thanks to names a cause of an outcome; courtesy of names a giver. In the ironic use the two converge exactly.
variants: by courtesy of
courtesy (bare, no of — normal American credit-line style)
entries.meaning: Credits the party that supplied, permitted, or provided the thing. Its native habitat is the small print under a photograph, but it has spread in two directions: as a neutral attribution of a source, and — far more common in speech — as a sarcastic attribution of blame. 1. Supplied or permitted by; with the permission of. 2. Caused by, usually ironic.
examples: All images courtesy of the National Archives unless otherwise noted.
Data courtesy of the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Dinner was courtesy of the hotel, which had lost our reservation twice.
We spent the night in Denver, courtesy of a mechanical problem in Phoenix.
The winning run came courtesy of a throwing error by the shortstop.
He has a scar over his left eye courtesy of a hockey stick and a bad decision.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈpɑrt ʌv/ · weak /ən ðə ˈpɑrt əv/ · casually /ən ðə ˈpɑrt ə/
entries.register: formal; legal, academic, and bureaucratic prose
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, always animate or institutional. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. With a pronoun most writers switch to the possessive construction: on his part, for my part.
entries.pattern: [abstract noun of behavior] on the part of [agent] / On the part of [agent], [clause]
entries.contrast: It hangs an agent on an abstract noun where by would be ambiguous: a failure by the board can be read as a failure the board caused, while a failure on the part of the board can only mean the board failed. Nine times out of ten the possessive is shorter and just as clear: the board's failure. Do not confuse it with on behalf of, which means representing, not committed by.
entries.meaning: Assigns the doer of an abstract action to the noun that names it. Whenever a nominalization has swallowed a verb — negligence, reluctance, misstatement, effort — the subject of that buried verb has to be reattached somehow, and this is the formal way to do it.
examples: The report found no wrongdoing on the part of the responding officers.
There was real reluctance on the part of the faculty to move the deadline.
Any misstatement on the part of the applicant voids the policy.
It took months of quiet work on the part of two staffers to get the language drafted.
An error on the part of the pilot does not by itself establish negligence.
The delay reflected a genuine failure of nerve on the part of the leadership.

entries.ipa: /baɪ ˈdɪnt ʌv/ · weak /baɪ ˈdɪnt əv/ · casually /baɪ ˈdɪnt ə/ · by itself has no weak form and keeps its full /aɪ/
entries.complement: noun phrase — characteristically abstract (effort, persistence, sheer luck, brute force) — or a gerund (by dint of working nights). Never a finite clause, never a to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: [clause] by dint of [noun phrase / verb-ing] / By dint of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Narrower than by means of. By means of takes an instrument or a procedure; by dint of takes exertion, stubbornness, or a personal quality. Not by dint of a crowbar, but by dint of brute force. Dint is a fossil meaning a blow or a stroke and survives only inside this phrase, which is why it is so often misspelled by dent of.
entries.meaning: Attributes an achievement to effort or to a quality rather than to a tool. It always implies that the thing was hard and that the doer supplied whatever was missing out of their own resources.
examples: By dint of sheer persistence she got the sealed records released.
He made the roster by dint of being the only left-handed catcher in three counties.
The town got through the winter by dint of two generators and a great deal of goodwill.
She made partner by dint of long hours and an unnerving memory for names.
By dint of repetition alone, the slogan started to sound like common sense.
They kept the paper alive by dint of not paying themselves for two years.

entries.ipa: /baɪ ˈminz ʌv/ · weak /baɪ ˈminz əv/ · casually /baɪ ˈminz ə/
entries.register: formal; technical, scientific, and legal writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (by means of dissolving the residue in acetone). Never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [clause] by means of [noun phrase / verb-ing] / By means of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: The long form of instrumental with and of method-marking by. Ordinary English says with a centrifuge; a patent says by means of a centrifuge, because with has too many other jobs. Against by dint of: means versus effort. Against via: via is compact and can also mark a route. Against using: using is the modern technical-prose default and is shorter.
entries.meaning: Names the instrument, mechanism, or procedure that produced the result. Its whole value is unambiguity: in a sentence where with could be read as accompanied by, by means of cannot be.
examples: The two fractions were separated by means of a benchtop centrifuge.
Access to the vault is controlled by means of a keycard and a four-digit PIN.
The signal reaches the valley by means of a repeater on the ridge.
He supported the family by means of a night job and two lodgers.
Payment may be made by means of certified check or wire transfer.
The sample was purified by means of passing it twice through a silica column.

entries.ipa: /baɪ ˈweɪ ʌv/ · weak /baɪ ˈweɪ əv/ · casually /baɪ ˈweɪ ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase; a gerund (by way of explaining himself); or — in the manner sense only — a bare article-less abstract noun: by way of apology, by way of introduction, by way of illustration. Never a finite clause of any kind, and never a to-infinitive: not by way of to explain.
entries.pattern: [clause] by way of [place] (route) / [clause] by way of [bare abstract noun] (purpose) / [clause] by way of [noun phrase] (means)
entries.contrast: Three jobs share one phrase and the complement tells you which is running. A place name means route and equals via. A bare abstract noun means as a form of and equals as. Anything else means means and equals by means of, which is usually cuttable — by way of illustration is just for example.
entries.meaning: 1. By the route of; passing through. 2. As a form of; for the purpose of, taking a bare noun with no article. 3. Through the mechanism of; by means of.
examples: We drove home by way of Flagstaff to get around the storm.
Mail from the islands still comes by way of Miami.
The flight goes to Managua by way of Houston and adds four hours to the trip.
By way of apology he sent a bottle of wine and a note that explained nothing.
She mentioned the lawsuit only by way of introduction and then moved on.
He put up a slide of the 1954 map by way of showing how little had changed.
The money reaches the districts by way of a county trust.
He learned Portuguese by way of two years in São Paulo and a patient landlady.
Complaints get to the board by way of an ombudsman nobody has ever met.

entries.ipa: /aʊt ʌv/ · weak /ˈaʊt əv/ and, at any ordinary speed, the two words run together as /ˈaʊtə/ — which is what the eye-spelling outta is transcribing, and the reason learners write out a curiosity
entries.register: neutral; one of the highest-frequency prepositions in the language
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or a fused relative (built out of what was left in the barn). A gerund occurs only in the motive sense treated in 06-cause-purpose (out of not wanting to embarrass her), and even there it grates. Never a finite clause and never a that-clause — not out of that he was tired. It strands as a unit, both words together: What is it made out of?, the fund the raise came out of — but the of can never be dropped and never left behind: not what is it made out?
entries.pattern: [verb of making] out of [material] / [number] out of [number] / [cost or payment] out of [fund or source]
entries.contrast: This entry owns the material, proportion, and funding-source senses. The spatial sense (out of the building) is in 04-movement-direction, the motive sense (out of spite, out of curiosity) in 06-cause-purpose, and the general all-senses entry in 11-complex-multiword. Against of for materials: made of oak names the substance and leaves it recognizable; made out of oak insists that raw stuff was transformed, which is why a table made out of a door is idiomatic and a table made of a door is not. Against from: from is the marker when the material is no longer visible in the product (wine from grapes, paper from rags), out of when it still is. Against in for proportions: one in five households is a rate over a population, nine out of ten dentists is a count taken from a stated set, which is why a test score is always 92 out of 100 and never 92 in 100. Out alone is an adverb and a verb particle (She went out, Cross it out, The fire is out) and takes no object at all, which is the test; the preposition is the two-word form.
entries.meaning: 1. The material a thing was made from, with the stuff still recognizable in the product. 2. Out of a stated set — the proportion sense, where both numbers are given and the second is the whole. 3. The fund or source a cost was paid from.
examples: He built the whole shed out of salvaged barn siding.
The bowl is turned out of a single piece of walnut.
She made supper out of whatever was left in the pantry.
Nine out of ten of the households surveyed had never heard of the program.
She scored ninety-two out of a hundred and was furious about the eight.
Three out of the four bridges on that stretch are rated structurally deficient.
The overtime came out of the general fund, not out of the grant.
Two of the positions are paid out of federal money that runs out in June.
He covered the difference out of his own pocket, which is the line the auditors underlined.

entries.ipa: /θru/ · no true weak form; in rapid speech the vowel shortens toward /θrʊ/ and, before a consonant, as far as /θrə/ (through the door /θrə ðə ˈdɔr/). The spelling thru is signage and shorthand, not standard prose.
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund (through working weekends for two years). Never a finite clause. It strands freely: the agency I found it through, Who did you hear it through?
entries.pattern: [clause] through [noun phrase / verb-ing] / Through [noun phrase], [clause] / stranded: the program I got the job through
entries.contrast: This entry covers the means and intermediary senses; the spatial sense is in 04-movement-direction, the inclusive-date sense in 05-time, and the fault-and-failing sense of number 3 is worked out in full in 06-cause-purpose. Against by: by marks the direct agent or the medium, through marks the channel that carried it — I heard it by phone is the medium, I heard it through a friend is the intermediary. Against via: near-synonyms for the intermediary sense, but through takes gerunds and strands where via does neither. Also an adverb and a particle — Let me through, We got through, I'm through with him — and there it has no object at all, which is the test.
entries.meaning: 1. By the means or method of — the process that produced the result. 2. Through the agency of; via an intermediary. 3. Because of, normally with a fault, an accident, or a lack.
examples: He built the business through twenty years of eighteen-hour days.
Most of our hiring happens through referrals rather than postings.
She got her start through working weekends at a station nobody listened to.
She got the loan through a credit union rather than a bank.
You can only reach him through his agent, and his agent does not return calls.
The house sold through a broker who never once set foot in it.
The mix-up happened through a clerical error, not through malice.
Through no fault of her own she ended up in the wrong terminal in the wrong city.
Two boxes of personnel records were lost through sheer inattention.

entries.ipa: /ˈjuzɪŋ/ · casually /ˈjuzɪn/ · no weak form — it keeps its own stress, which is one sign it is still half a verb
entries.register: neutral; the default in technical writing and instructions
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun. Never a finite clause, and — unlike a true preposition — it does not take a gerund: not using boiling the water. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [clause] using [noun phrase] / Using [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: A present participle that has drifted most of the way into prepositionhood. It competes with instrumental with and formal by means of, and technical prose prefers it because it names a tool without any of with's other meanings: Open the file with Sarah is ambiguous, Open the file using Sarah's account is not. Its participial origin still shows: when the main clause has no plausible user, you get a dangling modifier — Using a spreadsheet, the numbers were checked says the numbers used the spreadsheet.
entries.meaning: Names the tool, material, or resource an agent employed. It is the plainest instrumental marker English has after with, and unlike with it says nothing about accompaniment, possession, or manner.
examples: Tighten the bracket using a ten-millimeter socket.
The map was drawn using satellite imagery from 2019.
She paid using a card she had reported stolen the week before.
Using nothing but a paperclip, he got the battery cover off.
We track attendance using a shared spreadsheet nobody has permission to edit.
The team modeled the outbreak using three separate sets of assumptions.

entries.ipa: /ˈvaɪə/ · also /ˈviə/ (commoner in British English and in Latin tags) · no weak form: it carries a stress of its own, which is part of why it feels crisper than by way of
entries.register: neutral to formal; very common in technical and business prose
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun. Never a gerund and never a finite clause — not via sending an email. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [clause] via [noun phrase] / [destination] via [waypoint] / [noun phrase] via [medium]
entries.contrast: The travel-route sense is in 04-movement-direction; this entry is the medium and intermediary sense. Against by for media: by wants a bare article-less noun (by email, by phone) while via takes either (via email, via the app). Against through: identical in meaning for intermediaries, but through takes gerunds and strands and via does neither — the single commonest error with this word is putting an -ing form after it.
entries.meaning: 1. By way of a medium or channel of transmission. 2. Through an intermediary — a person, an agency, a system.
examples: Send the signed copy via email; the original can follow by mail.
Tickets are available only via the mobile app, which is the whole complaint.
Updates go out via text message and a recorded call.
The story reached us via a stringer in Ankara.
Payments clear via the ACH network, usually in two business days.
He got the interview via a former roommate who owed him a favor.

entries.ipa: /wɪð ði ˈeɪd ʌv/ · weak /wəθ ði ˈeɪd əv/ · casually /wəθ ði ˈeɪd ə/ — with reduces to /wəθ/ and the of to a bare /ə/, so the whole phrase can come out as three unstressed syllables around aid
entries.complement: noun phrase — an instrument or a person. A gerund is possible but rare and clumsy. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] with the aid of [noun phrase] / With the aid of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Against plain instrumental with: He read the inscription with a magnifying glass and with the aid of a magnifying glass mean the same thing, but the long form implies a difficulty overcome. Against by means of: by means of is neutral about difficulty and treats the instrument as sufficient; with the aid of treats it as assistance to an agent already working at it. Against using: using is neutral and modern.
variants: with the help of (the everyday form, commoner in American English, and the only comfortable choice with a person)
with the assistance of (the most formal; standard in official and academic prose)
entries.meaning: Marks an instrument or a helper that made an already-difficult thing possible. The agent stays firmly in the sentence's subject position and the aid is subordinate, which is exactly the difference from by.
examples: The worn inscription was finally read with the aid of raking light.
She walks now with the aid of a cane and a great deal of stubbornness.
With the help of two neighbors, they got the tree off the driveway before dark.
The bill passed with the assistance of four members of the other party.
He finished the manuscript with the aid of a small grant and a very patient editor.
Divers recovered the recorder with the aid of a remotely operated vehicle.

entries.ipa: /ˌɑ ˈlɑ/ · commonly reduced to /ə ˈlɑ/
entries.register: neutral to journalistic; knowing in tone
entries.complement: noun phrase, characteristically a proper name — a person, a work, a brand, a place, an era. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [clause] à la [proper name] / [noun phrase] à la [proper name]
entries.contrast: A compact in the style of. Against like: like compares anything to anything and asserts nothing about intent, while à la compares a way of doing to a known model and carries a whiff of imitation, homage, or parody. Against after the manner of: same meaning at the opposite register. Do not confuse the preposition with the frozen culinary nouns à la carte, à la mode, à la king, which take no complement.
variants: a la (unaccented, common in American copy; à la is the careful spelling)
entries.meaning: Says that something is done in the recognizable style of a named model. The name does the definitional work, so it has to be a name the reader already carries around — this is a preposition that fails completely on an unfamiliar complement.
examples: He gave a rambling hour-long press conference à la his predecessor.
The episode ends on a freeze-frame à la every sitcom made between 1979 and 1988.
She writes long comma-spliced paragraphs à la Kerouac and edits none of them.
They want a walkable downtown à la Portland, on a third of Portland's budget.
The team plays a switch-everything defense à la the 2015 Warriors.
He does the whole deadpan-narrator thing à la Wes Anderson.

entries.ipa: /əˈkɔrdɪŋ tu/ · weak /əˈkɔrdɪŋ tə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or a wh-nominal — either a fused relative (according to what the manual says, according to whoever answered the phone) or an embedded interrogative (according to how much water you use, according to which shift you are on). Never a that-clause, never any other finite clause, and never a gerund. The to here is a preposition and not the infinitive marker, so a bare infinitive is impossible too: not according to conserve water. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: According to [source], [clause] / [clause], according to [source] / [clause] according to [standard or plan]
entries.contrast: Two distinct jobs. As an evidential (according to the mayor) it reports someone else's claim and declines to endorse it — which is why according to me is odd and why attaching it to an obvious fact reads as sarcasm. As a manner preposition (according to plan, according to the rules) it means in conformity with and equals in accordance with and in keeping with. As per is the business-memo version of the conformity sense.
entries.meaning: 1. On the authority of; as reported by, where the source is somebody other than the writer. 2. In conformity with; in the manner prescribed by. 3. In proportion to; varying with.
examples: According to the medical examiner, the death was accidental.
Turnout was up nine points, according to preliminary county figures.
According to whoever answered the phone at the clerk's office, the filing window closes at noon.
Everything went according to plan until about the second hour.
Assemble the shelves according to the diagram on page four, not the one on the box.
Members are seated according to seniority, which takes longer than the vote does.
Rates change according to how much water you use.
Class size is set according to the age of the students.
The bonus is prorated according to what each office billed in the fourth quarter.

entries.ipa: /ˈæftɚ ðə ˈmænɚ ʌv/ · weak /ˈæftɚ ðə ˈmænɚ əv/ · casually /ˈæftɚ ðə ˈmænɚ ə/ — five syllables of which only two are stressed
entries.register: formal, literary; standard in art criticism and museum cataloguing
entries.complement: noun phrase, typically a proper name, a named school, or a period. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] after the manner of [model] / [noun phrase] after the manner of [model]
entries.contrast: The formal counterpart of à la and of manner like. Against like: like asserts resemblance, after the manner of asserts deliberate imitation of a method. In cataloguing the terms are graded and legally meaningful: by is autograph, attributed to is probably autograph, studio of means the workshop produced it, after means somebody else copied it later.
variants: in the manner of (commoner in American English and the form to prefer in ordinary prose)
after (bare, in museum and auction cataloguing: a later copy by another hand)
entries.meaning: Says that the thing was made or done in conscious imitation of a named model's method. Where à la is a quick comparison, this is a claim about how the work was actually made.
examples: He wrote a sequence of unrhymed sonnets after the manner of Berryman.
The chapel was decorated in the manner of the Venetian churches he had spent two years studying.
She argued the case after the manner of a prosecutor rather than a defense attorney.
The label read simply "Landscape with Cattle, after Cuyp."
The house rambles in the manner of a New England farmhouse that grew by accretion.
The score is orchestrated after the manner of the late Romantics, down to the doubled horns.

entries.ipa: /æz ˈpɚ/ · weak /əz pɚ/
entries.register: business and bureaucratic; disliked by every usage authority that mentions it
entries.complement: noun phrase only, almost always a document, an instruction, or a prior communication (as per your email, as per the contract). Never a gerund, never a wh-nominal, never a finite clause: not as per you asked, but as per your request — or better still as you asked.
entries.pattern: As per [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] as per [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: A redundant compound: per already means according to, so the as adds nothing, and commentators have called the phrase illiterate since the 1800s. In plain prose write per, according to, following, or nothing at all — as per our conversation is as we discussed. As per usual is a separate jokey idiom that is meant to sound wrong, and it is the one use nobody objects to.
entries.meaning: States that something conforms to an instruction, a document, or an established practice. It is pure register: it signals that the writer is operating inside a bureaucracy and is covering themselves.
examples: The deposit was refunded as per the terms of the lease.
As per your request, I have attached last quarter's figures.
Invoices are due within thirty days as per company policy.
The units were installed as per the manufacturer's instructions.
He turned up forty minutes late, as per usual.
Access was revoked as per the offboarding checklist.

entries.ipa: /laɪk/ · a full lexical word with no reduced form, though routinely unstressed
entries.register: neutral as a preposition; the conjunction use (like I said) is informal, and the approximative use is informal
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (like me, like her and me — never like I, never like she), a gerund (It's like flying), or a fused relative (like what happened in 2019, like whoever ran it last year). As a preposition it cannot take a finite clause and never a that-clause: like I said and like he does are the conjunction like, standard in American speech and casual writing and still edited out of formal prose in favor of as. It strands only in the fixed interrogative What is she like?
entries.pattern: [verb] like [noun phrase] / [be] like [noun phrase] / like [verb-ing] / Like [noun phrase], [clause] / fixed: What is X like?
entries.contrast: Against as, the classic split: like takes a noun and asserts resemblance, as takes a clause or a role actually held — She works like a lawyer means she resembles one, She works as a lawyer means she is one. The three-way ladder: Do it like me (everywhere), Do it as I do (formal writing), Do it like I do (standard American speech, flagged in formal writing). For examples, such as is the conservative choice because like can be read as resembling. Also a verb, noun, adjective, adverb, conjunction, suffix, and discourse particle — the preposition is the one with a noun-phrase object and no clause after it.
entries.meaning: 1. Resembling; in the manner of — the core sense. 2. Characteristic of; typical of, almost always with be and often negated. 3. Introducing an example. 4. Approximately, informal and spoken. 5. In the fixed question What is X like?, asking for a description. 6. Apparently, seemingly, after look, sound, feel, seem, smell, taste.
examples: He drives like a man who has never been ticketed in his life.
The fabric feels like raw silk and costs about a tenth as much.
Standing there in the doorway, she sounded exactly like her mother.
He was shaking like a leaf and pretending he was cold.
It is just like him to volunteer for a committee and then miss every meeting.
That is not like her at all — she is never late.
It would be just like the county to repave the street the week after the parade.
Bring something small: a paperback, a deck of cards, something like that.
Cities like Tucson and El Paso have been planning for this for twenty years.
We want something like what they built in Boise, only smaller.
The whole repair came to like four hundred dollars.
We waited like twenty minutes and then just left.
What is the new place like?
I have not met him. What is he like?
It looks like rain before noon.
That sounds like a plan nobody has thought through.

entries.ipa: /ʌnˈlaɪk/ · stressed on the second syllable, and no weak form
entries.type: compound (un- + like, no longer analyzed as two pieces) — also an adjective (two unlike quantities, unlike poles attract), where it takes no object
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun (unlike me), a gerund (Unlike renting, buying builds equity), or a fused relative (unlike what I said last week). Never a finite clause — not unlike I said; the repairs are unlike what I said or a contrastive conjunction such as whereas. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: Unlike [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause], unlike [noun phrase] / [be] unlike [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The negation of prepositional like, with two readings that split by position. Sentence-initial it sets up a contrast between two things filling the same role, and the two must be genuinely comparable or the sentence dangles: not Unlike most cities, Houston's zoning is minimal, but Unlike most cities, Houston has almost no zoning. Predicatively (That's unlike him) it means uncharacteristic. It is not the verb dislike, and not quite not like: He is not like his father denies resemblance in general, while Unlike his father, he... asserts a contrast on one named point. The litotes not unlike is a hedge meaning somewhat similar to. For the adjectival rival, American English writes different from, and different than before a clause; British different to does not belong in American copy.
entries.meaning: 1. In contrast to. 2. Not characteristic of; not resembling.
examples: Unlike her sister, she never learned to swim.
Unlike most of the coast, this stretch has no public access at all.
Unlike renting, a mortgage builds equity, at least in theory.
It is unlike him to leave without saying anything.
Her handwriting is completely unlike his, which is how the forgery was caught.
The new engine is not unlike the one it replaced, only quieter.

entries.ipa: /eɪ/ (stressed, citation form) · weak /ə/, which is the normal form here
entries.complement: a bare singular count noun of time, quantity, or measure: a day, a week, a head, a pound, a gallon, a person, a mile. Never a plural (not twice a days), never a gerund, never a clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [frequency] a [unit] / [price] a [unit] / [quantity] a [unit]
entries.contrast: This is not the indefinite article, even though it is spelled and pronounced identically. It descends from Old English on worn down to nothing — the same erosion that produced nowadays, asleep, ashore — and it means per. The test is substitution: twice a day is twice per day, never twice one day. Against per: identical in meaning, opposite in register — sixty miles an hour on the road, 60 miles per hour on the spec sheet. Never mix them: not per an hour.
variants: an (before a vowel sound: an hour, an ounce, an acre)
entries.meaning: Distributes a quantity over a unit. It is the most frequent rate marker in spoken American English by a wide margin, and it is invisible to most speakers, who take it for the article.
examples: She takes the medication twice a day with food.
Ground chuck was four dollars a pound that week.
He drives about eighty miles an hour on the interstate, which explains the three tickets.
Tickets were fifteen dollars a head at the door and twelve in advance.
The plant turns out two thousand units a week on one shift.
We were getting maybe three calls an hour by the end of the night.

entries.ipa: /æt ðə ˈreɪt ʌv/ · weak /ət ðə ˈreɪt əv/ · casually /ət ðə ˈreɪt ə/
entries.register: formal; standard in finance, contracts, and technical reporting
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a quantity — a number, a sum, a percentage, or a whole ratio phrase. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] at the rate of [quantity] per [unit] / [clause] at a rate of [percentage]
entries.contrast: The explicit form of rate-marking at, which is what plain prose uses: at 6 percent rather than at a rate of 6 percent. Against per: per names the unit, at the rate of frames the whole ratio, and the two normally appear in the same phrase. Do not confuse it with the idiom at this rate / at that rate, which takes no of and means if things keep going the way they are going.
variants: at a rate of (used when the rate is introduced rather than pointed back to; both are standard American English)
entries.meaning: Introduces an explicit ratio of quantity to unit. It is the register-marked version of what at, a, and per do more briefly, and it earns its length only when the ratio itself is the point of the sentence.
examples: The loan accrues interest at the rate of six percent a year, compounded monthly.
Water was coming into the hold at a rate of about forty gallons a minute.
Overtime is paid at the rate of one and a half times the base wage.
The glacier has been retreating at a rate of roughly thirty feet a year since 1998.
Bonds were redeemed at the rate of a hundred dollars on the thousand.
The state reimburses mileage at the rate of sixty-seven cents a mile.

entries.ipa: /pɝ/ (stressed, citation form) · weak /pɚ/, which is the normal form — the vowel is r-colored either way, so the unstressed form rhymes with the second syllable of water
entries.register: formal, technical, and commercial in the rate sense; the according-to sense is business jargon
entries.complement: in the rate sense, a bare singular noun with no determiner: per hour, per person, per capita, per unit — not per an hour, not per the hour. In the according-to sense it does take a determiner (per our agreement, per the memo). Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It can stand postpositively with the unit understood: forty dollars per.
entries.pattern: [quantity] per [bare unit] / [quantity] per (unit understood) / Per [document], [clause]
entries.contrast: Against a: identical in the rate sense, different only in register. Against for: four dollars per pound is a rate, four dollars for a pound is one transaction. Against as per: as per is this word with a useless as bolted on. Watch the Latin fossils, which keep the article-less rule: per annum, per capita, per diem, per se, per stirpes, and per cent — written as one word, percent, in American English.
entries.meaning: 1. For each — the rate sense. 2. According to; in accordance with, in business register. 3. Through; by means of, surviving mainly in commercial and legal formulas.
examples: The room is two hundred dollars per night, plus tax and a resort fee nobody explains.
Output is measured in barrels per day.
The state spends about twelve thousand dollars per student.
Income per capita has been essentially flat for a decade.
Delivery is nine dollars a box, or seven per if you order a pallet.
Per our agreement, the deposit is nonrefundable after Friday.
The forms were filed per the court's instructions.
Per the revised handbook, mileage is reimbursed only with a receipt.
The goods were shipped per the SS Marquette out of New Orleans.
Notice may be given per certified mail or per hand delivery.
Payment was remitted per the escrow agent named in Schedule B.

entries.ipa: /taɪmz/ · a full lexical word with no weak form; it keeps its own stress even between two stressed numerals (seven TIMES eight)
entries.type: simple (a plural noun reanalyzed as a preposition) — also the ordinary plural noun (three times a week, at times, the good times), which takes no complement
entries.complement: noun phrase — a number, a quantity, a measure noun, or a fused relative (three times what they paid). Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [number] times [number] / [number] times [the] [noun phrase] / [number] times [comparative adjective] / [number] times as [adjective] as [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: As a preposition it is the spoken form of the multiplication sign, and the phrase it heads is singular: Six times four is twenty-four, not are. Against by: dimensions take by (a three by five card), multiplication takes times. Against the -fold suffix: threefold attaches to the number, three times is a phrase. The classic ambiguity: three times more than and three times as much as are used interchangeably in American English, but strictly the first means 4x and the second 3x. Times in three times a week and at times is the ordinary plural noun, not this preposition.
entries.meaning: 1. Multiplied by — arithmetic. 2. Expressing a multiple or a ratio.
examples: Seven times eight is fifty-six.
Multiply the width times the height to get the square footage.
Twelve times twelve is a gross, which is the only place most people still meet the word.
The house is worth three times what they paid for it in 2011.
Rents downtown are nearly four times the county average.
She earns ten times as much as she did at her first job.
The new chip is roughly twenty times faster at the same power draw.

entries.ipa: /ə ˈmætɚ ʌv/ · weak /ə ˈmædɚ əv/ — the t is a flap, so it sounds like madder · casually /ə ˈmædɚ ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a small quantity, characteristically a stretch of time (a matter of minutes, a matter of a few dollars, a matter of inches). Never a gerund, never a finite clause in this sense. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [clause] in a matter of [small quantity] / [be] a matter of [small quantity] / only a matter of [quantity]
entries.contrast: The measure sense always means only that much, never that much or more — it took a matter of minutes says the job was quick, and it took a matter of nine hours is odd because nine hours is not small. That is the whole rule, and it is why the phrase cannot carry a figure the reader would think large. Do not confuse it with the topic noun in a matter of principle, a matter of public record, a matter of opinion, which names a category rather than a quantity and belongs with the prepositions of reference. Against in the neighborhood of: that phrase hedges a figure it does not know, this one belittles a figure it does.
variants: in a matter of (the commonest full form, and the one that carries the time sense: in a matter of hours)
it is only a matter of time (a frozen idiom meaning it will certainly happen eventually)
entries.meaning: Puts a small number on something in order to say how little of it there was. The figure is real, but the smallness is the point, which is why the phrase resists any quantity a reader would consider substantial.
examples: The fire went through the attic in a matter of minutes.
The whole difference between the two bids is a matter of a few hundred dollars.
He missed the cut by a matter of inches.
In a matter of three weeks the neighborhood had collected the entire amount.
Getting the permit turned out to be a matter of two phone calls and a fax nobody could send.
Whether the levee holds is now a matter of hours, not days.

entries.ipa: /əˈbaʊt/ · the first syllable is a bare schwa, and the whole word clips to /baʊt/ in casual speech: 'bout a hundred people
entries.register: neutral; the default hedge in both speech and writing
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity — a number, a sum, a measure, an age, a proportion. Never a gerund and never a finite clause in this sense. It does not strand. Also an adverb of degree (about right, about finished, just about done), where it has no object at all, and that is the test. About to leave is a near-future construction, not a prepositional phrase; a book about running is the topic word, treated at about.
entries.pattern: about [number] · about [sum] · about [measure] · about as [adjective] as [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: This entry covers the quantity hedge; the clock-and-calendar hedge (about seven, about three weeks) is at about and the topic sense at about. About claims to be close to the number, which is what separates it from the rest of the family: in the neighborhood of claims only the right range, on the order of only the right power of ten. Two habits to avoid: do not hedge a figure that is already exact (about 217 people undercuts itself), and do not stack it on a range, which is already doing the hedging — write forty to fifty people, not about forty to fifty people.
variants: around (the interchangeable twin, a shade more casual)
approximately (the lab-report register)
roughly (the neutral written alternative)
some (the terse journalistic one: some 200 people)
round about two hundred (British, not American)
entries.meaning: Hedges a quantity by a small margin. It is the most frequent approximator in American English and the one that carries the least attitude: it makes no joke, claims no precision it does not have, and is at home anywhere from a text message to an annual report.
examples: About two hundred people showed up for a room booked for eighty.
The repair came to about nine hundred dollars.
The tank holds about twelve gallons, which gets you to Tucumcari and no farther.
Attendance was about half what it was in 2019.
He is about six two, give or take an inch of hair.
The two proposals cost about the same and differ in every other respect.
About one in five households in the county has no broadband at all.

entries.ipa: /əˈraʊnd/ · clipped to /raʊnd/ in casual speech: 'round fifty bucks
entries.register: neutral to informal; a shade more casual than about
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity, a sum, or a measure. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand in this sense. Also an adverb and a verb particle (stick around, turn it around, the other way around), where it has no object — that is the test.
entries.pattern: around [number] · around [sum] · somewhere around [quantity]
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with about for quantities, with a mild division of labor: about is commoner with measured amounts and in formal writing, around commoner in speech and with round figures. Both claim to be close to the number. Against in the neighborhood of: the long phrase widens the tolerance and adds a folksy tone. The spatial and movement senses (around the corner, around the lake) are at around; the clock-and-calendar sense is at around.
variants: round is the British form and is not American English; an American writer uses around for the preposition and reserves round for the noun, verb, and adjective (a round of drinks, round the numbers off, a round figure)
'round (the contraction, belonging to songs and speech, not to edited prose)
around is also the American choice in year-round, around the clock, and the other way around
entries.meaning: Hedges a quantity, informally. It is the spoken default — in conversation Americans reach for it about as often as for about, and the choice between the two is rhythm rather than meaning.
examples: The truck goes for around forty thousand new.
They are expecting around fifty people, which in that family means sixty-five.
The building is around a hundred years old and has the wiring to prove it.
Enrollment has held steady at around twelve hundred since the mill closed.
We ended up somewhere around eight hundred dollars over budget.
He weighed around two-forty when they signed him and around two-ninety when they cut him.

entries.ipa: /æt ði ɪkˈspɛns ʌv/ · weak /ət ði ɪkˈspɛns əv/ · casually /ət ði ɪkˈspɛns ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (at the expense of getting any sleep). Never a finite clause. In the payment sense a possessive replaces the of: at the taxpayers' expense, at his own expense.
entries.pattern: [clause] at the expense of [noun phrase / verb-ing] / [clause] at [possessive] expense
entries.contrast: Three senses share a form. Sacrifice: speed at the expense of accuracy names what was given up. Payment: at the taxpayers' expense names who paid, and there the possessive is normal. Humiliation: a joke at his expense. Against to the tune of: both carry editorial weight, but to the tune of is about the size of a sum and this is about what the sum cost somebody.
variants: at the cost of (interchangeable in the sacrifice sense)
at a cost of (the only member of the family that takes a plain dollar figure)
entries.meaning: 1. With the sacrifice of; by giving up. 2. Paid for by. 3. At the humiliation of.
examples: The redesign gained speed at the expense of battery life.
He finished the degree at the expense of nearly every weekend for three years.
She built the department up at the expense of two smaller programs that got folded in.
The plant runs cleaner now, though at the cost of about eleven percent of its output.
The trip was made entirely at the taxpayers' expense, which is how it became a story.
Two of the flights were booked at the expense of the campaign committee.
The repairs were finally made at the landlord's expense after the second inspection.
They kept telling the same story every Thanksgiving, always at the expense of the same cousin.
The whole toast was ten minutes of jokes at the expense of the groom's driving.
He got the laugh, but at the expense of the one person in the room who could not answer back.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ɪkˈsɛs ʌv/ · weak /ɪn ɪkˈsɛs əv/ · casually /ɪn ɪkˈsɛs ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, essentially always a quantity or a named threshold. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [quantity] in excess of [threshold] / [clause] in excess of [quantity]
entries.contrast: A five-word way of saying more than, and in ordinary prose it should be cut: in excess of 200 people is more than 200 people. It earns its place in contracts and specifications, where over can be misread spatially and more than can sound like an estimate: amounts in excess of the deductible is unambiguous and amounts over the deductible is not quite. Against upward of: upward of is an estimate near the number, in excess of is a hard floor. Against north of: same meaning, opposite register.
entries.meaning: Marks a quantity as exceeding a stated threshold, with the threshold treated as a boundary rather than an approximation. Everything above the line is included and nothing below it is.
examples: The settlement was reported to be in excess of four million dollars.
Speeds in excess of ninety miles an hour were recorded on that stretch of road.
Any amount in excess of the policy limit is the insured's own responsibility.
The building has stood for a period in excess of two centuries.
Loads in excess of four hundred pounds will void the warranty.
Applicants with in excess of ten years' service are exempt from the review.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ði əˈmaʊnt ʌv/ · weak /ɪn ði əˈmaʊnt əv/ · casually /ɪn ði əˈmaʊnt ə/
entries.register: legal and commercial; distinctly American bureaucratic English
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a sum of money — figures or words. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [check / judgment / invoice / refund / bond] in the amount of [sum]
entries.contrast: Pure legalese for for or of: a check in the amount of $500 is a check for $500 and nothing else. It survives because in a document read adversarially it keeps the sum visibly separate from the instrument. Against to the tune of: same territory, opposite register and opposite attitude — the legal phrase is scrupulously neutral, the journalistic one is not.
variants: in the sum of (older; commoner in British legal drafting)
in the total amount of (for aggregates)
for (the plain-English replacement, and the one federal plain-language guidance recommends)
entries.meaning: Attaches an exact sum to a financial instrument or an obligation. It states the figure and takes no position on whether the figure is large.
examples: Enclosed is a check in the amount of twelve hundred dollars.
The court entered judgment in the amount of $84,317 plus costs.
We received an invoice in the amount of $2,415.60, which does not match the estimate.
A refund in the amount of the deposit will be issued within ten business days.
Bond was set in the amount of fifty thousand dollars.
The district issued notes in the total amount of nine million dollars.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈneɪbɚˌhʊd ʌv/ · weak /ɪn ðə ˈneɪbɚhʊd əv/ · casually /ɪn ðə ˈneɪbɚhʊd ə/
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity or a sum, or a fused relative standing in for one (in the neighborhood of what the appraiser said). Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in the neighborhood of [quantity] / somewhere in the neighborhood of [quantity]
entries.contrast: A hedge with a wider tolerance than about and a friendlier tone than on the order of. The three make different claims about precision: about $200 claims to be close, in the neighborhood of $200 claims only the right range, on the order of $200 claims only the right power of ten. Because it is folksy, it is out of place in a document where the number matters.
variants: in the ballpark of (more informal, also American, from the same family as a ballpark figure)
somewhere in the neighborhood of (the usual full form in speech)
in the region of (British)
of the order of (British)
entries.meaning: Gives an approximate quantity while explicitly declining to be precise. The metaphor is spatial and does real work: a neighborhood is a region, not a point, and the phrase concedes that the speaker has not measured.
examples: Repairs will run in the neighborhood of three thousand dollars, maybe a little more.
They are expecting somewhere in the neighborhood of forty thousand people.
The engine puts out in the neighborhood of four hundred horsepower.
He has been doing this for something in the neighborhood of twenty years.
The house sold for something in the ballpark of what the appraiser had said.
Attendance was in the ballpark of what we saw last spring.

entries.ipa: /ˈmaɪnəs/ · no weak form; the second syllable is already a schwa and the first keeps its stress
entries.type: simple (Latin, the neuter of minor) — also a noun (a minus, the minuses outweigh the pluses) and an adjective (a minus sign, a B-minus), neither of which takes an object
entries.register: neutral in arithmetic; informal in the lacking sense
entries.complement: noun phrase or numeral. Never a gerund, never a clause. It does not strand. In the temperature and negative-number use it is not really a preposition at all but part of the numeral, and there it takes no preceding quantity: minus forty, a minus sign.
entries.pattern: [number] minus [number] / [noun phrase] minus [noun phrase] / minus [number] (temperature)
entries.contrast: Against plus: exact opposites in arithmetic and mirror images in the informal sense. Against less: in commercial writing less is the standard subtractor for deductions (gross pay less withholding) and minus is the arithmetic one. American temperature convention: minus ten in writing, ten below in speech, negative ten in scientific and increasingly in general American use.
entries.meaning: 1. Arithmetic subtraction; reduced by. 2. Below zero — temperatures and negative quantities. 3. Without; lacking, informal and usually a little comic.
examples: Nine minus four is five.
Net proceeds are the sale price minus commissions and closing costs.
Enter the gross figure minus the two adjustments on line nine.
It was minus twelve in Fargo the morning they left.
The freezer holds steady at minus eighteen Celsius.
The wind chill hit minus thirty and the district held classes anyway.
He came back from the trip minus a suitcase and one shoe.
They played the whole second half minus their two best defenders.
The band finished the tour minus a drummer and most of their gear.

entries.ipa: /ˈnɔrθ ʌv/ · weak /ˈnɔrθ əv/ · casually /ˈnɔrθ ə/
entries.type: complex — bare north is a noun, an adjective, and an adverb (due north, the north side, drive north), none of which takes an object; only north of is the preposition
entries.register: informal; journalistic, especially in business and sports writing; American
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity — a sum, a number, an age, a speed — or a fused relative standing in for one (south of what the campaign was promising). Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] north of [quantity] / [noun phrase] north of [quantity]
entries.contrast: A live metaphor from the map, where north is up the page: north of $2 million is more than $2 million. Keep it out of formal writing, where in excess of or plain more than belongs, and well away from actual geography, where north of Denver means exactly what it says. Against upward of: upward of is an estimate, north of asserts a floor with attitude.
variants: south of (the mirror image, meaning less than)
entries.meaning: Puts a quantity above a stated number, informally and with a note of relish. The number named is almost always a round one, and the point is usually that it is impressively or scandalously large.
examples: The contract is reportedly worth north of forty million dollars.
He was still throwing north of ninety-five in the eighth inning.
Redoing the kitchen alone will run north of thirty thousand.
She is north of sixty and still runs half marathons.
Turnout came in south of what the campaign had been promising all month.
The stock closed south of nine dollars for the first time since 2019.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ði ˈɔrdɚ ʌv/ · weak /ən ði ˈɔrdɚ əv/ · casually /ən ði ˈɔrdɚ ə/
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity, usually a round number or a power of ten; in the second sense, a noun phrase naming a kind of thing. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the order of [quantity] / [noun phrase] on the order of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: In physics and engineering it has a technical meaning — within a factor of ten of — so on the order of a thousand legitimately covers a few hundred to a few thousand. In general prose it has weakened to approximately, and a scientific reader will still hear the stronger claim. Against in the neighborhood of: the neighborhood form is folksy and implies a narrower range. Do not confuse it with in order to, or with in the order of meaning in the sequence of.
variants: of the order of (standard British)
in the order of (British, and criticized there)
American English uses on the order of
entries.meaning: 1. Approximately; to within a factor of ten. 2. Of the same kind as; along the lines of.
examples: The device draws on the order of two watts in standby.
Losses were on the order of a hundred million dollars.
Sample sizes were on the order of ten thousand per site.
Recovery is expected to take on the order of six months.
What he has written is on the order of a very long apology.
She wants something on the order of a sabbatical, only paid.
The building is on the order of a warehouse with better windows.

entries.ipa: /ˈoʊvɚ/ · no weak form; the second syllable is a syllabic /ɚ/, and the flapped over a runs together as /ˈoʊvɚɹə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or a numeral; in the medium sense, a channel noun that normally keeps its article (over the phone, over the air, over a secure line). Never a gerund in any of the senses below and never a finite clause — the gerund-taking sense (sued over failing to disclose the defect) is the cause preposition in 06-cause-purpose. It strands (the number we came in over, what did you hear it over?), and it is also an adverb and a particle (Come over, It's over, turn it over), where it has no object — that is the test.
entries.pattern: [verb] over [quantity] / [be] over [budget / limit] / [number] over [number] (a fraction) / [verb of communication] over [the channel]
entries.contrast: This entry covers the excess-of-quantity senses and the transmission-medium sense. The others are spread across the catalog: the spatial senses in 04-movement-direction, the span-of-time and simultaneity senses in 05-time, the trigger-of-conflict sense in 06-cause-purpose, the preference sense (chose Denver over Phoenix) in 09-comparison-opposition, and the topic sense (a fight over money) in 10-topic-reference-role. Against more than: the old rule that over cannot mean more than with numbers was dropped by the AP Stylebook in 2014 and was never grounded in real usage. Against above: with plain counts over is the default (over sixty people), while above is preferred when the number sits on a named scale (above 30,000 feet, above average, above freezing). Against under: exact opposites here. The medium sense against the time sense: over dinner names a stretch of time you can measure, but over the phone names a channel and no stretch of anything, which is why we settled it over the phone in four minutes is fine and we settled it over dinner in four minutes is not. Against on: on the phone is the state of being connected, over the phone is the route the words took.
entries.meaning: 1. More than a stated quantity. 2. Exceeding a budget, a limit, or a standard. 3. Divided by — the spoken form of a fraction bar. 4. Through a channel of transmission — the medium sense, where the complement is the wire, the air, or the service that carried it.
examples: Over two hundred people showed up for a meeting the room was booked for forty.
Anything over fifty pounds ships freight.
The bridge has carried over a million vehicles since it reopened.
The project came in three weeks late and over budget.
We are eight hundred dollars over for the month and it is the fourteenth.
He was doing eighty in a fifty-five — twenty-five over.
Three over four is the same as seventy-five percent.
The odds were listed as one over twelve hundred.
He gave notice over the phone, which his father never forgave.
The warning went out over the emergency band twenty minutes before the sirens.
Nothing sensitive goes over email, and nothing at all goes over the hotel's wifi.

entries.ipa: /plʌs/ · no weak form; it is stressed even in four plus four, which is what keeps it audible in dictation
entries.type: simple (Latin, "more") — also a noun (a real plus, the pluses outweigh the minuses), an adjective (a plus sign, a B-plus), and a coordinating conjunction (Plus, it's cheaper), none of which takes a prepositional object
entries.register: neutral in arithmetic and pricing; informal as a sentence connector
entries.complement: noun phrase or numeral. Never a gerund in the arithmetic sense. The informal Plus, it's cheaper takes a whole clause, but that is a coordinating conjunction, not this preposition. It does not strand. Postpositively it attaches to a number with no complement at all: fifty-plus, a B-plus, thirty years plus.
entries.pattern: [number] plus [number] / [noun phrase] plus [noun phrase] / [number]-plus (postpositive) / Plus, [clause] (informal conjunction)
entries.contrast: Against minus: the arithmetic opposites. Against and: a plus phrase does not make a singular subject plural — The base rate plus the surcharge is eighty dollars, singular, is the careful form, exactly as with along with and as well as. Against positive: for temperatures, American English says ten above or simply ten, never plus ten, which is a European convention.
entries.meaning: 1. Arithmetic addition; increased by. 2. With the addition of — the price-and-package sense. 3. Postpositive: and more; at least that much.
examples: Four plus four is eight.
Enter the base salary plus any bonus in the second column.
Rent is eleven hundred a month plus utilities.
The fare is thirty dollars plus tip.
The venue holds five hundred plus.
She has thirty-plus years of classroom experience.

entries.ipa: /ˈʃaɪ ʌv/ · weak /ˈʃaɪ əv/
entries.type: complex (adjective + fixed of) — bare shy is an ordinary adjective (a shy child, don't be shy) and takes no object
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity, an age, or a point in time, or a fused relative standing in for one (just shy of what the board had authorized). Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It is nearly always preceded by a measure of the shortfall or by just.
entries.pattern: [size of shortfall] shy of [target] / just shy of [quantity]
entries.contrast: Means short of, not quite up to. Unlike short of, it has none of the exception senses: not shy of a miracle, we are finished. Just shy of is by far the commonest form and hedges downward. Note the collocational quirk: the phrase wants a measured gap in front of it, so shy of forty alone is odd where two months shy of forty is idiomatic. Against under and less than, which state a range; shy of states a near miss.
entries.meaning: Places a quantity just below a target, with the implication that the target was the thing being aimed at. The gap is small by definition, and naming it is most of the point.
examples: He died two weeks shy of his ninetieth birthday.
The bill came in just shy of four hundred dollars.
She finished a tenth of a second shy of the school record.
We ended up three votes shy of a majority.
The tank was a gallon shy of full when we got back.
The bid came in just shy of what the board had authorized.

entries.ipa: /ðə ˈbɛtɚ ˈpɑrt ʌv/ · weak /ðə ˈbɛdɚ pɑrt əv/ — the t of better flaps · casually /ðə ˈbɛdɚ pɑrt ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a divisible quantity — a stretch of time, a sum, a distance, a countable population. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. It does not strand.
entries.pattern: [verb of spending or lasting] the better part of [quantity] / for the better part of [stretch of time]
entries.contrast: It means most of, not the superior half of. The better is a fossil comparative meaning larger, the same one buried in the better half of the field, so the better part of an hour is about fifty minutes and says nothing about their quality. Two rules keep it honest: the complement has to be divisible (not the better part of a decision), and the phrase claims more than half and less than all, so it cannot be stacked on a hedge — not about the better part of a year. Against about: about a year may be over or under, the better part of a year is always under, which makes it a downward hedge from a round number. Do not confuse it with the proverb discretion is the better part of valor, where part means component and the whole thing is a different idiom.
variants: the best part of (the British form, which turns up in American speech as well)
the greater part of (the formal one)
most of (the plain replacement, and shorter every single time)
entries.meaning: Names most of a quantity while conceding it was not all of it. Whoever writes the better part of a million is telling you the figure did not quite get there.
examples: They spent the better part of a year waiting on the environmental review.
He drove the better part of four hundred miles without stopping once.
The better part of the crop was in the ground before the rain came.
The hearing took up the better part of two days and settled nothing.
She has lived on that street for the best part of thirty years.
Redoing the second floor ate the better part of the bequest.

entries.ipa: /tu ði ɪkˈstɛnt ʌv/ · weak /tə ði ɪkˈstɛnt əv/ · casually /tə ði ɪkˈstɛnt ə/ — both the to and the of reduce
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (to the extent of resigning). Never a finite clause — with a clause the phrase changes shape to to the extent that, which is a subordinating conjunction and a different item.
entries.pattern: [clause] to the extent of [quantity / noun phrase / verb-ing] / compare the conjunction: to the extent that [clause]
entries.contrast: Two readings sorted by the complement. With a number it is a measure and a ceiling: liable to the extent of $50,000 means that is the maximum. With an abstract noun or a gerund it means as far as, going so far as to. Do not blur it into to the extent that, which introduces a clause and functions as a conditional (= insofar as). Against in the amount of: that phrase fixes an exact sum, this one fixes an upper bound.
entries.meaning: 1. Up to a stated limit; to the maximum of. 2. Going as far as; to the point of.
examples: Each partner is liable to the extent of his capital contribution and no further.
The policy covers water damage to the extent of fifty thousand dollars.
The town rebuilt the levee to the extent of its available funds.
He backed her to the extent of putting his own name on the loan.
She disagreed, to the extent of filing a written dissent.
The company cooperated to the extent of turning over four boxes and then stopped.

entries.ipa: /tu ðə ˈtun ʌv/ · weak /tə ðə ˈtun əv/ · casually /tə ðə ˈtun ə/
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a sum of money, characteristically a large one. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] to the tune of [sum]
entries.contrast: Not a neutral way of stating an amount. It always carries an editorial nudge — that the sum is outrageous, wasteful, or improbably large. For a neutral figure use of or for; for a document use in the amount of. It resists small numbers, which is a reliable test: fined to the tune of forty dollars is comic rather than damning. The literal musical sense (sing it to the tune of "Yankee Doodle") is ordinary to plus a noun, not this idiom.
entries.meaning: Attaches a large sum to an action while signaling disapproval or astonishment. The metaphor is that the payer is dancing to somebody else's music.
examples: Taxpayers subsidized the stadium to the tune of three hundred million dollars.
The firm was fined to the tune of eleven million for the disclosure failures.
He ran up credit card debt to the tune of sixty thousand dollars in under two years.
The district overspent its transportation budget to the tune of about four million.
The settlement compensated the plaintiffs to the tune of twelve thousand dollars apiece.
The state has backstopped the fund to the tune of a billion and a half since 2018.

entries.ipa: /tu wɪˈðɪn/ · weak /tə wɪˈðɪn/
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a tolerance — a distance, a margin, a percentage. Never a gerund, never a finite clause. A trailing of + target is usually obligatory.
entries.pattern: [verb of measuring or approaching] to within [tolerance] of [target]
entries.contrast: One of the small set of stacked prepositions English allows (from behind the door, except in an emergency, until after lunch). It differs from plain within by adding a movement or a measurement that closes on the target: accurate within a millimeter states a standing property, machined to within a millimeter states a result achieved. Against shy of: shy of names a shortfall from a goal, to within names a tolerance around a target.
entries.meaning: Marks how close a process or measurement came to a target. The to supplies the movement and the within supplies the margin, which is why neither works alone in these sentences.
examples: The part is machined to within half a thousandth of an inch.
The final polls had it to within two points of the actual result.
They climbed to within a hundred yards of the summit before turning back.
Our estimate turned out to be good to within about five percent.
The clock keeps time to within a second a month.
The probe mapped the ridge to within a few centimeters of vertical accuracy.

entries.ipa: /ˈʌndɚ/ · no weak form; before a vowel the r links and the d flaps, so under an hour comes out /ˈʌndɚɹən ˈaʊɚ/
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or a numeral. Never a gerund in this sense, never a finite clause. It strands marginally (the figure we came in under) and is also an adverb (The whole block went under), where it has no object.
entries.pattern: [verb] under [quantity] / [be / come in] under [budget / limit] / under [age]
entries.contrast: This entry covers the below-a-quantity senses; the spatial sense is in 04-movement-direction. Against less than: interchangeable with plain numbers, though fewer than is the fussier choice for things you can count. Against below: under for plain quantities and thresholds, below for named scales and reference lines (below freezing, below sea level, below average, below cost). Against over: exact opposites. Note the separate subject-to sense — under warranty, under oath, under contract — which is not a measure at all.
entries.meaning: 1. Less than a stated quantity. 2. Beneath a budget, a limit, or a standard — the good kind of shortfall. 3. Younger than.
examples: Anything under twenty dollars they simply write off.
The whole crossing took under three hours.
The renovation finished two months early and under budget.
We came in under the county's noise limit at every measuring point.
Nobody under eighteen is admitted without a parent.
The program serves children under five and their caregivers.

entries.ipa: /ˈʌpwɚd ʌv/ · weak /ˈʌpwɚd əv/ · casually /ˈʌpwɚd ə/, which is why the -s of upwards is so easy to lose in speech and so audible on the page
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity. Never a gerund, never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] upward of [quantity] / [noun phrase] upward of [quantity]
entries.contrast: Two competing readings, and this is the word's real problem. Historically and in careful usage it means more than; in a great deal of current American writing it means approaching, as much as. A reader cannot tell which you intend, so when the difference matters write more than or nearly. Against in excess of, which is unambiguously a floor, and north of, which is the informal version of the same claim.
variants: upwards of (dominant British form, common in American writing too; American style guides prefer upward of, matching toward, forward, backward)
entries.meaning: Places a quantity at or approaching a stated number. It is the most ambiguous of the measure prepositions, and the only one in this section whose two readings point in opposite directions — which is why it should be replaced whenever the exact reading matters and left alone when it does not.
examples: The repair will take upward of six hours, so plan on the whole day.
Upward of twelve thousand people applied for four hundred jobs.
The equipment costs upward of a quarter of a million dollars.
They lost upward of half their inventory in the flood.
She has upwards of thirty years in the same building.
The hearing ran upward of five hours with no break.

entries.ipa: /wɪˈðɪn/ · also /wɪˈθɪn/ for some American speakers · no weak form: the stress is on the second syllable, and the with- inside it does not reduce to /wəθ/ the way free-standing with does
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun. Never a gerund and never a finite clause — not within finishing the job. It does not strand. It is also an adverb in legal and literary English (see within), where it has no object.
entries.pattern: [be / fall] within [tolerance or limit] / [verb] within [margin] of [target] / within [budget / reason / reach / one's rights]
entries.contrast: This entry covers the tolerance, limit, and distance senses; the deadline sense (within two weeks) is in 05-time. Against to within: within states a standing range, to within states a result measured up to a margin. Against in: in tolerance is shop floor talk and within tolerance is the written form; inside is spatial only. Against under, a real distinction: under budget means you spent less than the budget, within budget means you did not exceed it — and within includes spending every last dollar.
entries.meaning: 1. Inside a stated tolerance or margin. 2. Not exceeding a budget, a rule, or a right. 3. Inside a stated distance of something.
examples: Every reading was within tolerance except the one at station six.
The measurements came back within half a percent of the specification.
The department finished the year within budget for the first time since 2016.
Asking to see the file is entirely within your rights.
There are three hospitals within twenty miles of the plant.
He got within a stroke of the lead on Saturday and then fell apart on Sunday.
